iterations.theme: Counter-Arianism in politics and ecology as the first national minimum, with the beginning of a discussion on consensus about corporations and protectionism

sections.subtitle: Podcast number 115: pluralism without common foundations remains an empty word
sections.screenshot_description: Host Marin Marić opens the 115th podcast of the association Mladi za domovinu and introduces the guest Petar Šarić
sections.content:
The episode begins with a preview of selected quotes. In them, Petar Šarić speaks about the integration of migrants and about Croatia's role in Europe. He claims that "nobody has a clue" when someone is actually integrated: when they learn the language, when they start supporting the football national team, or when they forget their mother tongue. He describes Croatia as the "warrior caste of Europe" and "a cure for Europe", a country that is not small but "historical and decisive", without which "this continent would have fallen long ago".

Then the conversation itself begins. The host **Marin Marić** greets viewers at the 115th podcast of the association Mladi za domovinu. He starts from a paradox: in Croatia people gladly take pride in political pluralism and the growing number of parties, and every election cycle brings several new ones. At the same time, he says, this multitude does not help political discourse, because it is "increasingly poisoned" and reduced to base passions. As a consequence, he states that one cannot arrive at basic common assumptions about Croatian politics.

He introduces the guest as a philosopher and sociologist, a doctoral student at the Faculty of Philosophy in Ljubljana. **Petar Šarić** is the president of Svjetski savez mladih and of the association Atlas Hrvatska, and Marić assesses him as one of the greatest young intellectuals in Croatia. Šarić thanks him for the introduction and says that he is grateful and that he is looking forward to the discussion.

sections.subtitle: Civilizational minimums: not seeking coalitions, but a framework within which one can dispute calmly
sections.screenshot_description: Marić explains the goal of the conversation and the concept of civilizational minimums while Šarić listens
sections.content:
Marić sets the goal of the conversation: with Petar Šarić he wants to arrive at the "civilizational minimums" that must exist in Croatian politics for pluralism to be truly alive.

He immediately clarifies what he does **not** mean by this. He is not seeking "dazzling coalitions" nor that politicians of opposing worldviews hold hands and enter political battles together. He seeks a framework within which one can be calm, that is, within which politicians can debate while knowing that some basic assumptions are respected.

From this follows the backbone of the whole episode: confrontation is legitimate and desirable, but only within a common field about which there is no quarrel.

sections.subtitle: Worldview consistency in the age of postmodernity: politics of principles instead of politics of comfort
sections.screenshot_description: Šarić explains why people in the age of mass media lose their worldview orientation
sections.content:
Marić cites Šarić's column on the portal Mise u HR, which speaks about environmental protection and political ideologies and also touches on the topic of counter-Arianism. He relays its thesis that worldview consistency in the age of mass media suffers partly because of the oversaturation of the media space, which opens room for the mixing and confusing of perspectives. It also suffers partly because of the strategies of political elites and propagandists who opportunistically use such a state for their own benefit. According to Marić, people today position themselves mostly only in relation to the other side of the spectrum, without their own political passion.

Šarić agrees with this and places the phenomenon in the age of "political postmodernity", in which the great stories and great ideologies have been lost. People then lose the orientation of what their worldview should be. The consequence is that one day they argue one thing, and ten days later a completely opposite one, only because it is advocated by someone they do not find likeable or who does not belong to the circle with which they align.

In public advocacy, Šarić believes, one should be more oriented toward **principles**, and less toward the comfort of belonging. In practice this means: if someone truly believes in a principle, for example environmental protection, he must not reject it because the "other side" advocates it. Šarić asks why environmental protection would not be one of the principles that a patriotic perspective would also establish. He himself answers that this makes sense within every logic that can be represented there. He concludes that one needs to have the courage to hold to objective principles even when ideologies go along trajectories that put a person on the "wrong side" of what is normative for his group.

sections.subtitle: Counter-Arianism has two addresses: from Thompson's millions to the Zagreb railway and stadium
sections.screenshot_description: Marić cites examples of counter-Arianism on the left and the right, including the Zagreb city government
sections.content:
Marić confirms that counter-Arianism in Croatia is "very much growing". As an example from the area of the environment he cites the recent protest and the whole situation around Lika, where many positioned themselves only as being against something. First an example from the left: Thompson can invest a million or more millions of euros in something, and for the left it will still remain the "moral bottom".

Immediately afterwards he asks for honesty toward one's own side and says that there is this on the right as well. Whatever the city government in Zagreb does, even if it is objectively positive, there will always be a right-winger who will say that it does it badly, in a sectarian way, or too late. He notes that a decent stadium will be built on Kranjčevićeva, but it will be objected that it is not on time. The same holds for the extension of the railway, to which fault is again found. Marić emphasizes that he is not thereby defending the Zagreb government, but asks whether they must always be countered and criticized instead of being objective. If we disagree on many things and think diametrically oppositely, then wouldn't our thinking be more legitimate?

Šarić "absolutely" agrees. It would not occur to him either to legitimize the Zagreb government in countless things on which he would not agree with it. But if people want to do something objectively good, he asks why anyone would prevent them in that. One should retain "some minimum of reason and the well-being of society" and let the good happen, regardless of whether it is the government of the City of Zagreb, the government at the level of the Republic of Croatia, or the former government in Zagreb (Marić adds that "there was indeed" of that).

The first question regarding every political reality, Šarić claims, should be whether something is objectively good for people's lives, their children and future, and only then who these people are and what they previously advocated. If the first criterion is met, they should be supported, and if they need help, helped. He calls the principle "they are doing something good, let us try something bad" unproductive, because everyone wants the state and people's lives to be better. He asks for "psychological courage" so that a person does not bind himself to comfortable political frameworks that give belonging to a group that is against another. It is clearly seen, he says, when a person orients himself toward higher values, and not toward worldly ones that hold him in shackles.

sections.subtitle: Why new parties spring up: Foucault's politics of power and the disappearance of the question "what is good"
sections.screenshot_description: Šarić explains Foucault's idea of the politics of power as an explanation of counter-politics
sections.content:
Marić puts forward the thesis that the large number of parties is connected precisely with counter-Arianism. Few parties, he says, have a rounded political view and deal with concrete ideological principles, so each new one positions itself as against some other. As long as one goes against someone, there is always someone to counter, and in translation there are always many parties as well.

Šarić sees in this a reflection of a philosophical idea. He mentions **Michel Foucault** as a well-known representative of the "politics of power", for whom there is no objective truth or objective good in politics. There are only different camps and powers that try to present their action as good. According to this logic there is no objective good and it is up to us only to clash and gather enough power for something to become truth.

This is, Šarić claims, a reflection of the politics of "counter-I", in which the question of what is good for our society and our people is no longer the subject at all. The question becomes who said it and how one can go against him, so that one's own camp of power may come to the supreme position. If one is already speaking in binary divisions into left and right, Šarić concludes, this is an "inherently left-wing approach to reality", regardless of whether today it is advocated by someone who sees himself as a right-winger or as a left-winger.

Marić adds that one would expect right-wingers to look more at the objective good, and less at a subjective view of the other side. Nevertheless, polarization today takes place on the basis of affect and emotions, so-called affective polarization, without ideological consistency. Here, as the most concrete example of everything said, he announces ecology, and then other questions of consensus.

sections.subtitle: How the preservation of nature became a "brand" of the green left
sections.screenshot_description: Šarić explains the historical path of ecology from the hippie movement to the political brand of the green left
sections.content:
Marić asks how ecology became a synonym for the green left, even though it is about the protection of something universal, which has been present through the centuries, and how the left through the history of ideas took over this thought.

Šarić, with cautious words, "sketches" a time marker: it began somewhere in the eighties and nineties, and perhaps earlier, within the hippie movement. Then the so-called green left (Šarić emphasizes that these are broad, colloquial terms) began to use the rhetoric that it cares a great deal about the environment, that it loves nature and that it must be preserved. For Šarić these are "generally beautiful ideas".

The change came when these generations obtained political power and positions. The preservation of nature thereby became a day-to-day political issue advocated by the green left. In the background there also stood scientific theories that offer cataclysmic consequences supposedly arising from man's disrespect toward nature. In this way ecology has been "branded" for some twenty to thirty years already. Šarić believes that for most listeners the word ecology first brings to mind the green left with its green movements and actions. He concludes that it has become a brand, "and brand is existence".

sections.subtitle: Biocentrism or anthropocentrism: where is man in the story about nature?
sections.screenshot_description: Šarić criticizes biocentrism and advocates a healthily understood anthropocentrism founded on human dignity
sections.content:
Marić sees an essential difference in the view of the left and the right on the environment. With the left there is so-called **biocentrism** and an excessive veneration of nature above man. He recalls that Šarić wrote about the veneration of "mother earth".

Šarić first clarifies the point of the conversation. The fact that the preservation of the environment has become a brand of the green left does not mean that it is bad in itself, but just the opposite: it is something that is "objectively good by every principle". Everyone, regardless of political orientation, wants their children to drink clean water, play in a meadow and pick fruit from a tree, because they themselves also enjoyed these blessings. The question is only what the motive for preserving the environment is when viewed from the perspective of the green left, and what from the perspective of the patriotic right.

The ontology of the green left, according to Šarić, often takes the environment as a self-purposeful system, valuable in itself. This is seen in the idea of Gaia and mother nature, and even in something pagan. Šarić adds that they, if they contemplated more deeply, might not agree even with the idea of the existence of an objective good. To Marić's remark about how real pagans look at this, he replies that pagan practices were often animistic and venerated nature in order to explain everyday phenomena. He notes that he is not an expert in that, but that the parallel seems meaningful to him.

What is missing in that story is the position of man. When man is not included in the picture, one arrives at absurd theses, for example that the number of people on Earth should be reduced because people are carriers of a carbon footprint. Šarić calls this a manifestation of the **culture of death**, which completely flees from what should be the foundation of the desire to preserve the environment.

Therefore he openly advocates that every environmental protection be, to some healthy measure, **anthropocentric**. This means respecting human dignity, the value of man that is inherent to him and that neither any state nor the international community can either give or take away from him. If one starts from that point, man can by no means be a mere carrier of a carbon footprint. Nature is there so that man, in coexistence with it, while respecting human dignity, may use and obtain what he can, without destroying it. The reason is future generations and other people on the planet, who also have dignity and the right to use nature by the same mode.

sections.subtitle: Oikophilia and subsidiarity: love of home as a common point or a point of conflict
sections.screenshot_description: Marić asks whether Scruton's concept of oikophilia can be a meeting place of the ecological left and the traditional right
sections.content:
Marić refers to a column in which Šarić mentions **Roger Scruton** and his concept of *oikophilia*. He admits that he had not heard of the concept before, and he explains it as love of home that includes people, customs, culture and nature. He asks whether such a concept can be a meeting place of the ecological left and the traditional right.

Šarić says that he would be glad if it could, but before that one should consider what could prevent cooperation, which is currently quite topical in international ecological issues. Scruton writes under the motif of **subsidiarity**: the preservation of the environment is also the responsibility of local communities, of people who live in that environment, recognize its value, regard it as home and want to preserve it for future generations.

The approach of the green left, in contrast to that, often implies large international and global organizations, global plans and regulatory measures that would be imposed globally. There the conflict arises, because such institutions often become a battleground of various influences. Šarić gives a colloquial example: if within some international institution the theory is imposed that the consumption of meat is unsustainable and that it should be completely eliminated because of the carbon footprint of the industrial production of cattle, this may indeed be true. But if the theory slips into elite circles that are not free of the influence of corporations and other international actors, the danger appears that a regulatory measure "from above" (*top down*) will damage the quality and capacity of life of people in a local community who perhaps live from local cattle production.

The subject of disagreement is therefore the way of solving the problem: from below upward or from above downward. If one goes toward the common appreciation of the environment as a value, one should adopt the axiom that human dignity and man are at the center of the story, and not nature as "tremendously good" in itself. People should be given a certain level of autonomy and freedom. Šarić calls this subsidiarity and adds that it is also present in the social teaching of the Church.

sections.subtitle: From below or from above? Anarchists, Marx and Bakunin and the principle of "skin in the game"
sections.screenshot_description: Šarić explains how to reconcile global bodies and local actors with the principle of skin in the game
sections.content:
Marić warns that when it comes to ecology, the above–below division is not exclusively a left–right division. On the green left there are more and more anarchist movements and groups that demand the complete abolition of corporations and institutions, and yet one cannot escape the fact that occasionally global bodies need to exist. He gives the example of recycling: all individuals can recycle, but if large corporations package everything in plastic, individual recycling loses its meaning. People are not individualists who can look only at themselves, so something global must also exist.

Šarić agrees and first comments on the division into anarchists and advocates of solutions from above. It appears within the left paradigm from its beginnings. He recalls that for Karl Marx in the International the greatest enemies were anarchists led by Bakunin, a Russian theorist who advocated an anarchist version of socialism. They agreed on the materialist foundations, but not on whether the problem should be solved by international internationals or by people from below, with full freedom and a chaotic possibility of action. In the past, says Šarić, the advocates of international organizations mostly won, because they are more efficient in practice, while anarchists, by the nature of their ideology, are not particularly efficient when it is necessary to organize.

For contemporary practical action Šarić proposes a "golden mean" and admits that it sounds abstract, even paradoxical. Instances from above should exist, but their primary principle should be to **enable the action of those from below**. As a concrete manifestation he cites the motto of the European Union, unity in diversity: at the level of the EU every state should have the possibility of individual action and its own culture and of defining its own mechanisms for solving what is the subject of its action, while respecting agreed common things. In practice this diversity is lost, especially when great ideologies contrary to the interests of local producers and actors in individual countries are imposed from above.

Therefore, Šarić claims, one should seriously consider the principle that it is fine to define the problem from above and to emphasize the importance of its solution. But the foundation of every strategy must be that every individual actor who has "his skin in the game" (as the Americans would say, *skin in the game*) is asked what he is ready to contribute and to what limit, what destroys his possibility of survival, and how this can be avoided.

sections.subtitle: Nuclear energy: the quiet paradox of the green left
sections.screenshot_description: Šarić speaks about nuclear energy as a possible common point and the protest of Zelena akcija
sections.content:
Marić claims that every reasonable right-winger and left-winger can agree with the principle that Šarić set out, and that he will return to the geopolitical consensus later. He moves on to nuclear power plants as an example where both sides can be satisfied: that it be ecologically acceptable and yet productive, without a return to regression.

Šarić notes that he is not an expert in this area. From materials in the public space it seems to him that nuclear energy is an enormous potential that the green left for some reason often ignores and pushes into the background. As an example he cites the situation in the Republic of Croatia, when, according to his recollection, in the fourth, fifth or sixth month Zelena akcija protested against the efforts of the Ministry of Economy to launch projects for the production of nuclear energy in Croatia. At first glance this seemed absurd to him: nuclear energy is considered a sustainable, green type of energy because it does not imply the consequences of burning fossil fuels or a high carbon footprint, and yet it is not taken seriously.

Šarić also gives a historical framework. In the twentieth century nuclear energy was to a good extent considered the future, that which would raise humanity "to the stars", a great promise. That promise at some point simply subsided.

Marić sees counter-Arianism here as well: depending on who proposes the nuclear direction, the other side must be against, because it does not trust him. He admits that certain risks exist, but with responsible management, he says, we know that it is the most efficient.

sections.subtitle: Sociology of risk: why we fear airplanes, and not cars
sections.screenshot_description: Šarić explains the culturally conditioned perception of fear using the example of black holes, airplanes and cars

sections.subtitle: Why ecology matters to the right as well: a debt to future generations
sections.screenshot_description: Šarić summarizes why a right-winger should care about ecology, with Marić's statement about the first national minimum
sections.content:
Marić notes that they have moved away a little from the basic left–right division, so he asks for a short summary to close the topic of ecology: why is it important that a right-winger also cares about ecology?

Šarić answers personally and generationally. All who were born in the twentieth century, or just after it, enjoyed the blessings of natural life. Everyone has memories of walking in a park, playing on the grass and hanging out with friends in nature. Some drank water from the tap or ate homemade tomato from grandma's garden. He believes that we owe it to future generations to enable the same experience, i.e. "that we do not pollute the environment in which we live" and do not destroy it because of great global promises of profit and GDP growth. Or "because someone paid well to dump waste in the suburb of our city". One should preserve what the ancestors "defended with blood and left behind".

For Šarić this is not at all an ideological question, but a common-sense one, and it is absurd to ignore it only because someone else at some point advocated it, and by other principles is ideologically incorrect. The lesson is that one should deal with concrete, objective topics. The goal is to defend the objective good, and not to fight against what someone advocates only because one wants to fight with him. A fight at certain moments can be a necessary means, but it is not something from which one should draw pleasure by setting oneself against groups only because they exist.

Marić concludes that with this they have "managed to politically determine some first national minimum", although, as he ironically notes, no one asks us. He announces that political actors will come to the podcast and that, as elections draw closer, they will be asked questions about the basic consensuses on which everyone should agree.

sections.subtitle: Corporations as a social phenomenon: a topic that does not belong only to the left
sections.screenshot_description: Šarić lists the negative effects of corporations as a second issue on which the left and right should agree
sections.content:
Marić asks what first comes to Šarić's mind regarding other questions, besides environmental protection, on which the left and right simply must agree.

Šarić answers that it is the **negative effect of corporations** in general. It is often considered that this topic is reserved for left-wing currents, because the negative effects of corporations on citizens are tied to workers' rights. Šarić believes that this is not necessarily a perspective tied to workers' rights, but a social phenomenon that should be objectively analyzed. When one looks beneath the worldview surface of the neo-conservative right, one finds there too concepts and tools for assessing whether there is a negative effect of corporate and industrial action. He mentions here a term that ASR writes as "umbrella capitalism".

According to Šarić, Croatian society has gone through many historical ailments, including socialism, and still suffers from some things, perhaps even those that came from the West. The West definitely was not a better alternative to socialism, but it too brought its own problems. Today international corporations dictate the international labor market and the opportunities on it, they dispose of enormous amounts of capital, which gives them the power to shape people's lives in unpredictable ways.

Šarić believes that citizens who democratically elect their representation must have the power to prevent corporations from acting to the detriment of the quality of their everyday lives.

sections.subtitle: Healthy protectionism: an entire neighborhood must not be sold to a foreign corporation
sections.screenshot_description: Šarić and Marić discuss healthy protectionism toward Croatian citizens
sections.content:
Concretely, says Šarić, this would mean that an international corporation perhaps should not be allowed to buy an entire neighborhood in Zagreb when it is put up for sale. Croatian citizens should be given a certain level of **privilege**. He cites this as one of the dimensions of the problem.

Marić tries to summarize: every political option should have some kind of protectionism toward the Croatian people and the Croatian state. Šarić confirms "absolutely", with a reservation: he does not think that the people should seek some "political catharsis" and shift responsibility to the state. Every person, he emphasizes, should on an individual level try to secure what is vitally necessary for him. But those who work in government must think about what level of protectionism would be appropriate so that international actors with their power do not damage the quality of life of the citizens whom politicians represent.

Marić, in defense of domestic politicians, notes that in Croatia there is at least a public consensus that everyone is to some extent for protectionism and that there are no prominent libertarians. Partly this is, he says ironically, because party cadres have to be employed somewhere. He concludes that "healthy protectionism" is nevertheless needed.

sections.subtitle: Market freedoms under the magnifying glass: tomato, real estate and the question of the free flow of people
sections.screenshot_description: Šarić considers the freedom of flow of goods, capital and people and gives the example of a tomato and real estate
sections.content:
Šarić moves on to more general market freedoms: the freedom of flow of goods, people and capital.

**Flow of goods.** Local producers want to place themselves on the market and perhaps offer a better-quality product than the international producer. It is, however, hard to compete in price with international producers who perhaps have lower and worse criteria. The standard libertarian premise is that people will decide rationally and buy the cheaper or better product. Šarić objects that buyers often do not have a comprehensive body of information. An example is a tomato that is 10 cents cheaper than another. The buyer perhaps does not know who collects the profit, in what conditions it was produced, whether pesticides were used or whether there are health risks. Therefore he believes that assisted local production should be a principle by which we do not leave ourselves entirely to the free market of goods.

**Flow of capital.** With foreign investments Šarić highlights the issue of enabling foreigners to buy real estate in Croatia, which can raise prices. This is a problem for a young person who wants to afford a property. At the same time, a large part of people use real estate as a store of capital, so opening the market at the international level would only increase this problem.

**Flow of people.** The third dimension he calls perhaps the most problematic, especially in the context of mass migrations.

Marić follows up that this will be a burning topic at every next election in Croatia. The questions of foreign workers and obtaining citizenship will certainly have those who are more for and those who are more against, which is legitimate. Then he asks Šarić what, when it comes to demographics and migrations, should be a consensus about which there is no debate.

iterations.theme: Migration, human dignity, security and the geopolitical position of Croatia in Europe

sections.subtitle: Reversed order: when the left defends the free market and the right opposes it
sections.screenshot_description: Petar Šarić explains that on the question of migration the ideological positions of the left and right are swapped
sections.content:
Marin Marić opens the second large block of the conversation with a question that will, as he assesses, be a „burning topic“ at every next election in Croatia: foreign workers, obtaining citizenship and the division into those who are for and those who are against. He is interested in what, in the matter of migration and demographics, should be a consensus about which there is no debate.

Petar Šarić immediately warns that this is a „very tricky question“. In his opinion, the left–right division is not clear here, mostly because in the Croatian context the situation is **completely reversed** in relation to the classical economic ideological positions. What is colloquially called the right is skeptical toward an absolutely free market that would import migrants. The left, on the other hand, increasingly calls for morality and the need to bring in migrants, although the argument itself is actually **of a market nature**, because it is said that labor force is needed on the labor market.

Šarić sees in this a confirmation of the thesis from the beginning of the conversation: political ideologies today have lost their orientation and „float in the in-between space“, so they advocate what seems appropriate to them at a given moment, and not consistent principles.

As a possible source of common ground Šarić cites the question of why foreign population is imported at all. One of the justifications is that the labor market needs workers who will work cheaply, so that local employers do well in business, and citizens have cheaper services and goods.

sections.subtitle: The „exploit“ argument: who is coming to save the Croatian pension system?
sections.screenshot_description: Petar Šarić criticizes the thesis that migrants save the pension system
sections.content:
Petar Šarić emphasizes that such an approach „is certainly not an approach that respects any excessive human dignity“. It is often sold as a great moral act, as if people are being enabled a better life and a great gain, but in practice this is, according to Šarić's words, **an attempt at state-market exploitation** and at keeping unsustainable systems alive.

He particularly refers to the frequent claim that the pension system collapses if migrants are not imported to save it. Šarić asks: „Which migrant comes to Croatia with the aim of saving our pension system?“ In his opinion, the solution for an unsustainable system should be sought elsewhere, and not in exploiting people as a potential economic gain of the local state.

From this he draws the conclusion that all moral arguments in favor of economic migrations „fall into the water immediately“. The only real argument that is actually presented is, as he calls it, the **„exploit“ argument**. Šarić sees this as a possible point of contact that both sides of the political spectrum could respect.

sections.subtitle: Referendum, quotas and the question of „Croatian lineage“: what is citizenship at all?
sections.screenshot_description: Marin Marić speaks about quotas and opposition to the quick acquisition of citizenship
sections.content:
Once it has been established that the only real argument is material benefit, the question arises of how to position oneself toward this practically. Petar Šarić proposes: if we already believe in the „illusory fact“ that we live in a democratic society, then a **referendum** should be called on whether Croatian citizens want the import of foreign population. According to his general knowledge of public opinion, he believes that citizens would not advocate the method of integration, but would rather opt for **abstinence from the import** of foreign population.

Marin Marić believes that the majority would nevertheless be for some kind of **quotas**, because in conversations with people he gets the impression that it is generally thought that Croatia lacks workforce. The majority would, however, be against a foreign worker being able to become a Croatian citizen „overnight“. Marić is convinced that foreign workers will over time increasingly obtain citizenship, and some are already obtaining it, and he asks what the minimal consensus would be on how someone can become a citizen.

Šarić distinguishes two questions. Citizenship is, according to his description, a „mere legal basis“: the state defines the conditions, and whoever fulfills them becomes a citizen. The question that is considerably more complex is **when someone actually becomes a member of the Croatian people**, that is, when he integrates into society, whether he can be integrated at all and which groups integrate more easily and which with more difficulty. He assesses that in this debate there are many „mystical terms that promise a lot and solve little“.

sections.subtitle: Excavator and spoon: is the need for workforce objective?
sections.screenshot_description: Petar Šarić uses the example of an excavator and spoons to illustrate the idea that the need for workforce is ideological
sections.content:
Petar Šarić announces that he would like to „disappoint“ some of those mystical terms, and the first is the **need for workforce** itself. He asks whether it is objective or a socially conditioned term that gives an appearance of security.

For illustration he uses a vivid example: if it is necessary to dig a deep pit and ten thousand workers are needed for it, and each gets a spoon and diligently digs, everyone will receive a wage. But someone should have been smart enough to call an **excavator** that will do the job for a fraction of the price. Marin Marić adds that everyone thinks the excavator is expensive, and Šarić agrees that it is expensive and complex. Nevertheless, people are often not inventive enough to think that a machine would very quickly solve what a crowd of workforce solves over a long time.

Šarić admits that the example is simplified, but concludes that employers should be more oriented toward **innovation** and the rational organization of the enterprise, and not toward solving every problem by accumulating workforce. The objective need for workforce, he says, is only that quantity of problems that could not be solved without it.

He also notices a contradiction in the public space. The media daily bring news about artificial intelligence and automation because of which everyone will lose their job, and at the same time the need for workforce grows. Šarić asks what is then actually being automated if the need for workforce remains inexhaustible. He concludes that it is an „ideological conception“. Development should remain within a rational framework that does not fall into transhumanism, which would again go against human dignity. The great need for workforce is actually covertly the need to maintain an unsustainable pension system or to maximize GDP. Šarić asks whether these indicators are good enough to sacrifice for them „the fate of the Croatian people“.

Marin Marić follows up that progress is inevitable and that automation will in the long term always be cheaper than cheap workforce. He raises the question of what will happen with the foreign workforce once automation happens, and a large number of workers has already been accumulated.

sections.subtitle: The secret of sociology: nobody has a clue when someone is integrated
sections.screenshot_description: Petar Šarić reveals that there is no consensus on when someone is integrated
sections.content:
Petar Šarić moves on to the concept of **integration**, which, according to his words, sounds magical and is often heard in the statements of political elites: „we will integrate these people“, „they will integrate when they arrive“. Such rhetoric, he says, gives a person an appearance of security.

As someone who comes from sociology, Šarić shares a „secret“: **nobody actually has a clue** when someone is integrated. There is no general consensus on whether it would be when he has learned the language, when he has started supporting the football national team, or when he has forgotten his mother tongue. It is unclear in which situation a person truly becomes integrated.

He also honestly admits what he himself considers a reliable confirmation of integration. He sees it as possible only in rare cases, for example when there is a **common enemy**, as in wars. Historically speaking, peoples united and lived in coexistence when they had a common threat. Today such an environment, according to Šarić, does not exist, and no one would even want an enemy because of which they would have to unite with people who have migrated here.

sections.subtitle: Who is to blame for the import? The responsibility of elites and misunderstood migrants
sections.screenshot_description: Petar Šarić speaks about the responsibility of the elites who opened the door to mass migrations
sections.content:
Petar Šarić then analyzes the approach that the right has toward migrants and warns of one problem. He believes that the problem is not that migrants are often perceived as a „malicious entity“, as if they had come in order to clash with the local population. In his opinion, the great majority of them came for **purely materialistic reasons**: to earn money, to send it to their families, and those who want to stay count on their children receiving a better education. He doubts that the majority come with the intention of spreading Sharia law. That would, he says, be an „eventual generational consequence“, and not a motive for arriving.

A realistic approach, Šarić believes, starts from the fact that these people have been imported and that the question of responsibility must be posed elsewhere. They are not to blame for having followed a mere material instinct. Perhaps those are to blame who considered that the import was a good strategy at that moment, and ignored the potential negative consequences, which are known:

- the problem of **ghettos and isolation**,
- conflicts with the local population,
- a feeling of insecurity among the locals,
- a general loss of security in an area.

Šarić assesses that the elites who decided to open the door to the mass import of migrants probably had these scenarios on the table and concluded that it is a „worthwhile price to be paid“. He clarifies that he is not necessarily speaking about Croatia, but in general about countries that imported migrants.

sections.subtitle: Common denominator: progress, dignity of the person and equal labor rights
sections.screenshot_description: Marin Marić summarizes a possible consensus on progress, dignity and the labor rights of foreign workers
sections.content:
Marin Marić summarizes what has been set out up to then and asks for a general political consensus. First, he believes that everyone can agree that no one is against **progress** and development: if the economy grows, let it grow, but a more sustainable way of that growth and of automation should be found. Second, everyone should agree on the **dignity of the human person**.

In concrete policies this would, according to Marić, be reflected in **labor rights**. If foreign workforce were guaranteed equal rights, with regard to accommodation, wages and working conditions, far fewer employers would decide on the import. Marić asks whether Šarić thinks that more attention should be devoted to labor rights and the social policy of labor.

Šarić honestly admits that he has not thought much about it. He assumes that the set criterion of normal living conditions for foreign workers would make them not so profitable for the employers who motivate their import, so the import might also decrease. He assesses this as a „real possibility“ and an interesting idea, but asks for more time to think it over before a concrete judgment. Marić proposes that this be a topic for the next podcast.

sections.subtitle: Dignity or rights: where is the real political battlefield
sections.screenshot_description: Petar Šarić explains the difference between transcendent human dignity and human rights
sections.content:
Petar Šarić follows up and emphasizes that he has thought a lot about the concept of **human dignity** as a possible point of contact. He believes that the fundamental disagreement between the left and right currents is that the right is more ready to acknowledge that human dignity is **transcendently conditioned**, that is, that the value of man is in some way „God-given“ and surpasses every worldly, human power. The left perspective, according to him, would more respect the concept of **human rights**, which are a material international convention.

Šarić sees in this „the real political battlefield“ of the discussion about what has priority, dignity or rights. What is key, he believes, is that the thesis be accepted that human dignity is **the condition of human rights**, and not the other way around, i.e. that rights exist because the state guarantees them.

He explains why this is important. If everything is reduced only to human rights, without a transcendently founded dignity, then they can, by social convention, that is, by international law, be completely erased or changed. If, however, dignity is acknowledged, these rights cannot be arbitrarily changed, and if the most powerful international actors change them, human dignity still remains the measure by which such a change can be judged.

sections.subtitle: Rounding off the migration consensus: GDP versus the safety of the streets
sections.screenshot_description: Petar Šarić argues that the material benefit from migrations is not worth the sacrifice of security
sections.content:
Marin Marić asks that, after the touched-upon topic of dignity, the consensus on foreign workforce be rounded off. Petar Šarić confirms that one should agree on the claim that it is not a moral story about importing workforce, but exclusively the **„exploit“ argument**: people are imported for the sake of a promised material benefit. He proposes that one should then first examine whether this benefit exists at all and at the expense of what.

Šarić goes through these promises:

- **Maintaining the pension system.** For him it is „obvious“ that this is not a solution and that the solution should be sought elsewhere.
- **Maximization of GDP** and the glorification of the fact that immigrants pay taxes. He believes that by the very import of foreign workforce the ethical settings of a people are called into question, so he asks whether this is a sacrifice that the people are ready to bear for „mild economic promises“ of GDP growth.

He illustrates this with a question that he would put to the average Croat: does he need a mild GDP growth or would he rather preserve **the safety of his streets** and the future of his children, and even the very perception of the safety of the space in which he lives. Šarić believes that the latter would be more precious to him. Thus the materialist reasons for motivating mass migrations too „fall into the water“.

He also adds the story of the „fairy tale“ of the need for workforce and concludes that one should concentrate on innovation, and not on the exhaustion of people from the third world. Marin Marić agrees and calls this exploitation, against which, he believes, all reasonable people are.

sections.subtitle: Security consensus: investment in the army and the paradox of the left
sections.screenshot_description: Petar Šarić speaks about the need for investment in the army and the stance of the left toward the order
sections.content:
Marin Marić moves on to security as the next topic of the common good and notes that here too there are great disagreements, especially about the powers of the police and the army, although in Croatia the distrust toward these institutions is less than in America and some Western societies. He asks how to determine a minimum of respect for and preservation of security.

Petar Šarić answers that one should advocate the argument of **long-term rationality**. One cannot expect the security situation of a state to be stable if decisions are continually made that call it into question. One of them can be the import of foreign workforce, and another insufficient **investment in the army** and the military survival of the people. Šarić refers to the assessment that „the popularity of the world is declining“ and that global geopolitical security is ever weaker, so the more meaningfully we invest in the army, the greater the chance that the „blessing of life“ will persist for us in the form to which we are accustomed. He believes that everyone should agree on this by common sense.

He also looks back at the left, whose position seems to him „mildly paradoxical“. In his opinion, it considerably **profits from the current order**, which legitimizes much of what it has advocated for decades. Nevertheless, when this order faces a challenge, for example from Russia or China, it still in some way obstructs the investment in the army that could defend it. Šarić sees here a „loss of meaning“.

He also returns to migrations. He states that the people who are imported often have values in radical discrepancy with the values of the green left, which nevertheless advocates the moral argument that they should be brought in and enabled to prosper. Šarić believes that this left should be told that the people whose import it uncontrollably advocates do not tolerate the ideology that it tries to manifest in this society.

Marin Marić summarizes: one can debate about methods, for example about compulsory military service and the percentage of GDP, but everyone should be for investment in the security system.

sections.subtitle: Nuclear energy, local production and a strategy for the age of fewer Croats
sections.screenshot_description: Petar Šarić speaks about sustainable production, energy and demographic strategy
sections.content:
Petar Šarić emphasizes one more dimension that is not exclusively security-related, but is extremely important for security: **local production and energy sustainability**. He recalls that the Croatian economy depends considerably on tourism. Assuming that this is at least temporarily good and that Croatia currently enjoys a privileged position, a huge profit comes from tourism, which becomes an investment for the development of the rest of the country. The question is, however, whether this money is being invested in something that will make the country **sustainable in the long term**.

As an example he cites energy and the previously mentioned nuclear energy: would not investing currently available funds in it ensure the sustainability of Croatia in the coming decades? Šarić believes that the country often concentrates on superficial goals that bring immediate well-being, and ignores what ensures long-term survival.

This leads him to demographics. Everyone, he says, agrees that as many Croats as possible and a higher birth rate are desirable, but one must be realistic: this is a question that is very hard to solve and it is not certain whether it will be strategically solved in the coming decades. Therefore a strategic question arises: **what if there will be two million fewer Croats in forty years?** The answer is, according to Šarić, investment in self-sustaining production. Needed are one's own energy production, a stable army that is invested in, and production at the local level. This is what enables survival for a smaller people that is becoming even smaller, and after several decades, he adds, „who knows“, perhaps there will again be more and more of them.

sections.subtitle: Multipolar world: defending the West without closing one's eyes to its weaknesses
sections.screenshot_description: Petar Šarić speaks about the advantages and weaknesses of the West in the context of Croatia's positioning
sections.content:
Marin Marić notes that the world is increasingly breaking into a multipolar order, which opens new topics and consensuses. Croatia has long been part of Euro-Atlantic integrations, but Marić has the impression that **eastern influences** are increasingly appearing and that not all parties have a vision of Croatia as a Western state. He asks whether this should be made conscious again and agreed upon.

Petar Šarić advocates a „sober approach“ that respects both the weaknesses and the advantages of the West. Among the weaknesses he lists **decadent ideologies**, the consequences of an uncontrolled migration policy in the urban environments of the West and the fact that, as he says, destructive ideologies are for some reason continually pushed, especially at the level of the European Union.

But once these weaknesses are made conscious, one should also recognize the positive sides. People in the **Atlantic-Western NATO framework** have by far the best quality of life. Croatia is moreover tied to the logical historical continuity of Europe, which Croats too have defended for centuries, even millennia. He concludes that the Croatian place is logically in the West, which currently provides protection and enables the maintenance of „some kind of sovereignty“.

sections.subtitle: The myth of Russia as the promised land of tradition and advice: remain loyal, but have a backbone
sections.screenshot_description: Petar Šarić criticizes the romanticization of Russia as an alternative to the West
sections.content:
Petar Šarić criticizes those who sympathize with **Russian or Chinese influence**. In his opinion, they very soberly see the problems that he listed, such as decadence and mass migrations, but become ignorant toward the positive side of the West. He calls this a „cheap ontological guarantee“: when the West has decadent elements, it is declared the worst thing ever, and one immediately moves toward others.

Šarić ironically notes that in this way one can forget that in Russia too there is no lack of decadent elements. He mentions **high rates of abortion and divorce** and emphasizes that Russia is not a „promised traditional society“. He recalls that it was a socialist country, a constitutive part of the USSR, and that the political elites until some thirty years ago still persisted in that framework. The romanticization of alternatives to the West, he concludes, goes in a problematic direction.

Croatia should have a strategy for how, while staying in the West, to avoid the negative effects of decadence and mass migrations and preserve autonomy. This also means that, when one sits down at the table in the European Commission, one must „gather courage and say no“. Šarić at the same time admits that the current political elites too have an elaborated logic: one hundred percent loyalty to the West ensures that Croatia will be invited to the table. He also cites the example that behind a Croat in a random African country stands the whole European Union, which does not hold for a Montenegrin in the same situation, and this is a prestige that one must know how to appreciate. Nevertheless, he emphasizes, one must keep a „backbone“ and know what the values and role of Croatia are in the global geopolitical order, which is very often forgotten.

sections.subtitle: „The warrior caste of Europe“: Croatia as a cure for the continent
sections.screenshot_description: Petar Šarić explains that Croatia is a cure for Europe and that its backbone must be returned to it
sections.content:
Marin Marić agrees that the backbone should be preserved, but believes that this would be easier if Croats more strongly became conscious of belonging to Europe, and not through a **transactional view** that they often hear from politicians („we got this from Europe“, „we lost that“). A broader awareness is needed that Croatia is civilizationally, culturally and religiously a part of Europe and that through history it was with reason on its rampart. Marić asks whether a deeper awareness is lacking and whether „third-world“ conceptions of Europe as the universal evil of the white man who colonized the world have crept in.

Petar Šarić answers that the role of Croatia in contemporary Europe is to accept its fate and history as a **constitutive part of Europe**. Instead of asking how to come to an agreement with the European powers and begging Germany and France for technology and strategies, one should ask what the Croatian contribution is and why Croatia is at the table at all.

The answer is, according to him, clear: „we are the warrior caste of Europe“, those who were the **defenders of European values**. Croatia is a people that to a great extent is still connected with the Catholic, Christian understanding of the world, it has not lost its connection with spirituality or with patriotism. Therefore, he claims, it is „a cure for Europe“. Europe needs the return of a backbone, and Croatia can give it to her. Its role is not only to sit at the table, but to **have the main say** and to remind France, Germany, Britain and others of the objective principles that they have, as he assesses, forgotten. Šarić concludes that Croatia is not a small country, but „historical“ and „decisive“, and that „this continent would have fallen long ago if it were not for us“. Marić assesses that this is perfectly summarized.

sections.subtitle: Homeland War, Turks and centuries on the rampart: why Croats underestimate themselves
sections.screenshot_description: Petar Šarić speaks about the historical role of Croats in the defense of Europe and about external influences
sections.content:
Marin Marić asks whether Petar Šarić thinks that a feeling of inferiority and influences (such as musical ones) because of which Croats think they are worth less are being pushed in a planned way, through services.

Šarić confirms that there are certainly some such dimensions. He recalls that **during the Homeland War** many great Western powers hesitated with the recognition of Croatia as a state, among them Great Britain and perhaps France. Therefore there are global geopolitical actors skeptical toward Croatia and inclined to see it in the background. But this, he claims, does not justify the Croatian „spineless“ position. He believes that these actors too can be brought to sobriety and that today's political action carries much of the burden of the alliances from the First and Second World Wars.

Therefore, according to Šarić, one should free oneself of this and recall a **deeper European history**. The First and Second World Wars, as against five centuries of defense from the Turks, seem to today's Croats the most important events, but in a period of two to three thousand years there are more essential ones. He cites the Punic Wars, the Greco-Persian wars, the five-hundred-year defense from the Turks and the Crusades, which lasted for centuries and defined the continent. Croats should recall their role in these stories, at least since they have existed.

Marić states that every politician should hear this: Croatia must acquire a consensus that it is a part of Europe, but with a backbone, that no one can drag it away and that it must not be subservient to anyone. Šarić adds that Croatia, when it comes to the table and keeps silent, „betrays Europe“, that is, what she needs from it: a new signpost to survival.

sections.subtitle: Three points without which there is no debate: what politicians should respect
sections.screenshot_description: Petar Šarić sets out three points that politicians should respect in debates
sections.content:
Marin Marić sets Petar Šarić a hypothetical task: that he run a media grouping, that before the elections he organize many debates and that he tell politicians that some things are unchangeable and will not be debated. Šarić answers with three points:

1. **Ecology.** Nature is a good of the Croatian people that must not be sacrificed at any price. „Someone's foreign waste in the yards where our children pick fruit“ will not be dumped. He hopes that everyone can agree on this.
2. **The future of the people ahead of abstract measures.** The future of the Croatian people will not be sacrificed for corporate goals, for abstract indicators such as GDP, or for promises of maintaining a pension system that is in itself unsustainable. Instead, **alternatives and innovations** are sought.
3. **The Croatian place in Europe.** It is high time that Croatia take on its „fateful place“ in the future of Europe, its role and duty. It should not suffer from being the lowest at the table, but should „stand on the chair“ and fulfill its function toward the continent that Croatia has already defended countless times and that will, in Šarić's words, if need be, defend even from itself.

Marin Marić assesses that this would be excellent if it were respected. He announces that when politicians come to the podcast, he will ask them what they think about these points, and notes that with this only a series of topics of national interest has been started.

sections.subtitle: Politics begins with the individual, and pluralism lives within a common framework
sections.screenshot_description: Petar Šarić says that political change happens through personal life and kindness toward one's neighbors
sections.content:
Marin Marić at the end recalls personal responsibility: it is not only global policies that are being discussed, but one must change also from the personal side.

Petar Šarić confirms that everything starts from the **individual** and the way he lives his life. To greet a neighbor, to do the good that is possible, to be good and merciful toward the people in one's life, that is, he says, „a greater and more enormous political action“ than any going out to elections and advocacy. There is always a dimension of **apostolic action**: if people are truly good, believe in the objective good and do not look only for a subject of quarrel with other groups, this is reflected on others and causes positive change in the societies in which they live. Šarić's message is: „Be good, work out, live healthily, be good toward your neighbors and political change will simply come by itself.“

Marin Marić thanks the guest and recalls that they could hear why he called him at the beginning one of the greatest young intellectuals in Croatia. In the concluding thought he emphasizes that **pluralism** does not mean that all values are equally good or that everyone must „hold little hands“. Pluralism means that people can have different views, opinions and philosophies, but within a common framework of national and human interest about which everyone must agree. With this, along with the wish that the podcast be interesting, the conversation was concluded.
